opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it gets at a real tension in the field right now.

When people talk about learning from human data, the most direct version is behavioral cloning: you watch a person do a task, you record their hand motions or whatever proxy for actions you can extract, and you try to map observations to actions directly. The problem is that humans and robots have very different bodies. Our hands have far more degrees of freedom than most grippers, we move at different speeds, we have different reach and different senses. So if you treat human video as action labels, you immediately run into the embodiment gap. You end up spending a lot of effort on retargeting, and even then the actions often don't transfer cleanly.

The world-model view asks a different question. Instead of "what action did the human take, and how do I copy it," it asks "what did the human's interaction teach us about how the world works?" When a person opens a drawer, pours water, or folds a towel, they reveal a lot about physics, object affordances, and which state changes are possible and meaningful. That knowledge is largely independent of whose hand caused the change. A drawer slides the same way whether a person or a robot pulls it.

So in the world-model framing, human data is mainly a source of information about dynamics and outcomes: how objects move, what intermediate states look like, what a successful task looks like. The robot then figures out how to achieve those transitions with its own body, through planning, through a smaller amount of robot-specific data, or through reinforcement learning against that learned model.

I'd also say the two aren't strictly opposed. In practice you often want both. Human data can give you a strong prior over what to do and what the world will look like, and a bit of robot data grounds that in the robot's own action space. But the key distinction is what you treat as transferable. Behavioral cloning bets that actions transfer. The world-model approach bets that understanding of the world transfers, and I think that bet scales much better as we move toward collecting huge amounts of everyday human experience, from egocentric video, wearables, and so on, where we'll never have perfectly aligned robot actions.

r002.rationale: It mentions egocentric video as one source of human experience, but does not state that first-person video alone suffices; it also discusses wearables and robot-specific data.

r003.rationale: It describes recording human hand motions or action proxies and mapping observations to actions, conveying the relationship between sensory observations and actions required for behavioral cloning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important distinctions in how we think about learning from humans right now, and it gets conflated a lot.

Behavioral cloning treats a human demonstration as a label. You see a state, the human took an action, and you try to regress onto that action. The implicit assumption is that the human is an oracle policy, and your job is to copy it as faithfully as possible. That works surprisingly well when you have lots of data and the test distribution looks like the training distribution. But the human is not actually a policy you want to copy verbatim. Humans are noisy, they're multimodal, they take different paths to the same goal, and critically, they're solving the task with a body and a perception system that are not the robot's.

The world-model framing flips what you're extracting. Instead of asking "what action did the human take," you ask "what does this demonstration tell me about how the world works." A human video of someone opening a drawer is not a drawer-opening action label. It's evidence about how drawers respond to force, where handles are, what happens to objects inside when you pull. That knowledge is agent-agnostic. It transfers across embodiments in a way that action labels fundamentally cannot, because there is no human action that maps cleanly onto a robot's joint space.

So in practice we use human data to learn the dynamics and the affordances, the structure of the environment and how it evolves, and then we let the robot figure out its own actions against that model. The human becomes a source of physical and semantic priors rather than a source of supervision on motor commands. That also changes how you handle failure. In BC, a mistake is just an error you hope to average out with more data. In the world-model setting, a mistake is informative. It tells you something about the model being wrong, and you can go collect data in exactly that regime.

I'd also say the world-model view is more honest about what the data contains. Most human video on the internet has no action labels at all, and it has no reward signal. If your only tool is behavioral cloning, that data is essentially useless to you. If your tool is predictive modeling, that's the richest dataset on earth. So part of this is pragmatic. The approach that lets you use the data that actually exists at scale is the one that wins.

r003.rationale: It describes behavioral cloning as mapping states to actions, but does not explain that it requires capturing the relationship between human sensory inputs and actions.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is what you’re trying to learn from the human. In behavioral cloning, you’re treating the human as an example of what the robot should do: given this observation, take this action. But human actions don’t map directly onto robot actions. We have different bodies, different hands, different capabilities.

With a world model, you’re trying to learn how the world changes. If someone picks up a cup or pushes an object, that observation tells you something about objects, interactions, and the consequences of actions. The human is providing evidence about the world, rather than necessarily providing an action the robot should copy.

Then the robot can use that understanding to figure out how to achieve an outcome with its own body. The challenge is making that knowledge actionable: watching a human move an object doesn’t automatically tell the robot which motor commands will produce the same result. So you still need to connect that learned understanding to the robot’s own experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is what you’re trying to learn from the human. In behavioral cloning, you’re learning a policy: given this observation, what action would the human take? The human provides examples of the behavior you want to reproduce.

With a world model, you’re trying to learn how the world changes: if an action happens in this situation, what happens next? Human behavior becomes evidence about objects, interactions, and the consequences of actions. Then a robot can use that understanding to choose actions for its own goal, rather than simply imitate what the person did.

That distinction matters because humans and robots have different bodies and capabilities. A robot may not be able to copy a human’s motion, but it can still learn something useful about what that motion accomplishes. The challenge is making sure the model actually understands those consequences well enough to guide the robot’s actions.
